title: A disynaptic trigeminal circuit for the transformation and integration of oral chemesthesis in male mice
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
Chemesthesis, encompassing oral sensations such as spiciness and coolness, is an important yet incompletely understood component of mammalian chemical sensing. Unlike taste or olfaction, these sensations are conveyed primarily through trigeminal pathways; however, how modality-specific peripheral signals are processed and transformed along central ascending pathways remains poorly understood. Herein, we delineate the structural and functional organization of an ascending trigeminal-brainstem-parabrachial circuit that mediates oral chemesthetic processing in male mice. Using viral tracing, in vivo calcium imaging, and chemogenetic and optogenetic manipulations, we identify a genetically defined disynaptic glutamatergic pathway (trigeminal ganglion → spinal trigeminal nucleus caudalis → lateral parabrachial nucleus) that is both necessary and sufficient for capsaicin- and menthol-evoked defensive behaviors. Although peripheral TRPV1
                    +
                    and TRPM8
                    +
                    neurons retain a degree of modality bias, we observe substantial convergence of spicy and cooling signals within the spinal trigeminal nucleus, followed by sustained and synchronized population activity in
                    vglut2
                    +
                    neurons of the external lateral parabrachial nucleus. This hierarchical transformation from peripheral segregation to central integration reveals the organizational principle by which distinct chemesthetic modalities are progressively integrated along a trigeminal-mediated ascending pathway, providing a circuit-level framework for understanding how chemical stimuli are processed and coordinated to drive defensive behaviors.

title: Direct regulation of a tRNA modification enzyme by ppGpp links stress signaling to translational control and biofilm development
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
Transfer RNA (tRNA) modifications influence decoding efficiency and translational fidelity, yet how they are integrated into bacterial signaling networks remains poorly understood. Here, we identify a direct connection between stress signaling and codon-specific translational regulation. We show that the alarmone guanosine tetraphosphate (ppGpp) directly inhibits MnmE (TrmE), a conserved tRNA-modification GTPase required for methylaminomethyl (mnm) modification of wobble uridine. High-resolution ribosome profiling in
                    Bacillus subtilis
                    revealed that loss of MnmE selectively increases ribosome pausing at AAG codons and reprograms translation of a subset of genes, including small open reading frames. Among these is a previously unrecognized AAG-containing leader peptide that controls expression of the biofilm repressor AbrB. Consistent with this mechanism,
                    mnmE
                    mutants exhibit constitutive extracellular matrix production and bypass the biofilm defect of a
                    relA
                    mutant. Together, these findings establish a pathway linking ppGpp signaling, tRNA modification, codon-specific translation, and multicellular development.

title: Rapid activation kinetics of the NLR Swordholder underpin nonhost resistance to Phytophthora capsici in Nicotiana tabacum
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
Nonhost resistance (NHR) represents a durable phenomenon where plants resist nonadapted pathogens. While NHR holds substantial potential for engineering crops with broad-spectrum and durable resistance, its underlying molecular mechanism remains incompletely understood. The oomycete pathogen
                    Phytophthora capsici
                    is nonadapted to
                    Nicotiana tabacum
                    (Nt) but is virulent on the closely related
                    Nicotiana benthamiana
                    (Nb). Here, we demonstrated that both species encode the NLR Swordholder (Swh), which recognizes
                    P. capsici
                    AvrNt effector proteins. NtSwh restores NHR in
                    ntswh
                    mutants, whereas NbSwh confers only partial resistance. Mechanistically, NtSwh exhibits weaker autoinhibition mediated by its amino-terminal extension domains, enabling rapid immune signaling that prevent pathogen effector–mediated suppression; NbSwh’s stronger autoinhibition delays activation, permitting effector suppression. Heterologous expression of NtSwh in tomato enhances field resistance to
                    P. capsici
                    without yield penalty. These findings indicate that the kinetics of NLR can play a key role in defining NHR, in addition to the presence or absence of specific NLRs, providing insights into strategies for breeding durable crop immunity.

title: Human carotid plaque risk imaging using multiparametric photoacoustic and ultrasound fusion (hCAPRI)
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Assessing the risk of carotid plaque rupture remains limited because current imaging methods cannot provide both plaque composition and structural information in real time. Here, we present human carotid plaque risk imaging (hCAPRI), a multiparametric photoacoustic and ultrasound (PA/US) fusion method for real-time carotid plaque assessment. hCAPRI combines PA imaging for detecting intraplaque hemorrhage (IPH) with US imaging for evaluating the plaque structure. PA imaging measured IPH size and methemoglobin content, while US imaging assessed stenosis severity, calcification, and plaque thickness. Combining these PA/US parameters, we compute an hCAPRI score. In 171 carotid arteries (CAs) from 120 patients, hCAPRI revealed the relationships among the PA/US parameters. In 36 CAs validated with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), hCAPRI showed high agreement with MRI. The hCAPRI score achieved 89% sensitivity and 84% specificity for high-risk plaque classification. hCAPRI offers a low-cost, real-time, and contrast-free approach for carotid plaque risk imaging.

title: Lighting up necrotic neurons from traumatic brain injury with magnetic quantum dots to decode the cellular origin of MRI
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
The diagnosis of traumatic brain injury (TBI) remains heavily constrained by the limitations of conventional imaging techniques in visualizing the pathological events that determine the disease progression and outcome. To address this clinical challenge, we report a manganese-doped near-infrared quantum dot (QD) to intrinsically integrate the highly sensitive optical imaging with clinical compatible magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Taking the advantages of optical imaging powered by whole-brain clearing and cellular resolution three-dimensional (3D) panoptic imaging, in combination with the systematic in vitro cell studies on different types of cells involved in TBI, we disclosed the interpretable pathology reflected by TBI imaging through the highly sensitive fluorescence of magnetic QDs, i.e., after systemic administration, the nanoprobes were extravasated through the compromised blood-brain barrier and then selectively phagocytosed by activated microglia, which subsequently migrated into the regions rich in dead neurons and neuronal debris. This microglia-mediated tropism decodes the signal origin of MRI enhanced by the nanometer-sized contrast agent, thereby transforming the MRI from an anatomical tool into a pathological reporter. A biocompatible Fe
                    3
                    O
                    4
                    nanoparticle of similar size was also compared with the magnetic QD mentioned above for validating the translational merits of nanoparticles in MRI diagnosis of TBI.

title: Massively parallel self-assembly of suspendable microcompartments for functional cell screening
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Modern biology increasingly demands platforms that can compartmentalize and analyze single cells and cell-cell interactions at massive scale, yet existing compartmentalization strategies based on microfluidics suffer from critical limitations. Emerging lab-on-a-particle technologies such as nanovials enable anchored single cells or small groups of cells to be isolated and assayed in a fully suspendable and parallelized manner using standard instrumentation, although their open architectures can result in loss of growing or un-attached cells. Here, we introduce capped nanovials: self-assembling hydrogel compartments formed by docking spherical capping particles into bowl-shaped nanovials. We routinely achieve capping of >80% of all nanovials in a sample and >90% sorting yield by flow cytometry, making the capped nanovial system well-suited for preparing and running large-scale assays. Furthermore, we demonstrate stable clonal expansion of single mammalian, yeast, and bacterial cells; growth-based selections of >10,000 colonies; enhanced signal-to-noise in secretion assays; and high-purity selection of antibody-secreting cells based on activation of co-encapsulated T cell reporters (>30-fold signal, up to 100% selection purity). By combining the simplicity of a well plate with the functional precision of droplet microfluidics without requiring oil or custom instrumentation, capped nanovials realize accessible, high-throughput, and high-resolution experimentation.

title: Dynamic redox reactivation of platinum sites for long-term glycolate electrosynthesis from polyethylene terephthalate wastes
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
Glycolates are indispensable in the health, chemical and pharmaceutical industries, whereas their mainstream production involve toxic chemicals and harsh operating condition. An alternative route for glycolate production is electrifying ethylene glycol (EG) that originates from polyethylene terephthalate (PET) but suffers from poor durability of active platinum site that tend to deactivate. Herein, we demonstrate a dynamic redox reactivation strategy, which alternates between working potential for oxidizing EG to glycolate and nonworking potential for reviving active platinum sites by the chemical reduction of adsorbed EG, realizing an unprecedented stability for over 3000 hours under average current density of ∼220 milliamperes per square centimeter. Upscaling this approach, the assembled electrolyzer drives a record current of 10 amperes at 1.18 volts for repeatable 40 batches of glycolates electrosynthesis, with each batch converting 48.0 grams of PET to 11.6 grams of glycolates (52.8% yield), 37.7 grams of
                    p
                    -phthalic acid (95.8% yield), 248.7 grams of NaHSO
                    4
                    (95.2% yield) and ∼11.5 liters of hydrogen, showcasing a considerable revenue of ∼$1072 per ton glycolate.

title: Accumulated radicals by GHz femtosecond burst drive one-step superhydrophobic conversion
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
Short-lived radicals usually decay before they can drive long-range reactions, making laser-induced radical chain reactions difficult to sustain. Here, we used GHz femtosecond bursts to temporally couple excitation events, allowing reactive intermediates from preceding subpulses to remain available for subsequent reactions and favoring their transient accumulation relative to isolated-pulse excitation. Consistent with this temporally coupled process, the methylphenyl silicone resin/graphene/CuFe
                    2
                    O
                    4
                    /SiO
                    2
                    composite coating exhibits a threshold-like nonlinear wettability transition near 430 subpulses. Compared with the microsecond-spaced single-pulse femtosecond regime, the sub-nanosecond GHz burst produces more extensive chemical conversion, enabling one-step bond reorganization and phase transformation and yielding a low-adhesion superhydrophobic surface with a contact angle of 161° ± 0.7° without posttreatment. Pulse-timing–controlled radical-mediated chemistry thus provides a time-domain strategy for ultrafast materials synthesis.

title: Mechano-electrochemical energy harvesting and self-powered sensing via dynamic liquid metal–electrolyte interfaces
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Wearable devices, stretchable sensors, and soft electronics benefit from harvesting ambient energy using compliant materials, yet existing approaches often face limitations in power density, scalability, and electrode adaptability. Here, we report a liquid metal mechano-electrochemical energy harvester (LMMEEH) that converts mechanical stimuli into electricity through dynamically regulated electrode-electrolyte interfaces. Mechanical motion changes the interfacial area and drives asymmetric Faradaic reactions associated with dynamic oxide formation and dissolution, generating electrical output. The fluidity, high surface tension, and self-renewing surface chemistry of liquid metals enable rapid interfacial reformation, large reversible deformation, and stable cyclic operation. The device achieves a power density of 140.2 microwatts per square meter and scales to a 40-unit array producing 2 volts. Spatial and temporal programming of the liquid metal interfaces further enables synchronized three-phase alternating-current generation. We demonstrate wave-driven emergency lighting, self-powered pressure sensing, and real-time physiological monitoring. This work establishes dynamic liquid metal electrochemical interfaces as a scalable strategy for soft mechanical energy harvesting and self-powered electronics.

title: Defining epidemiologically relevant units of cholera transmission in sub-Saharan Africa
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Much remains unknown about cholera transmission dynamics in Africa. Applying both traditional phylogeographic techniques and innovative methods for combining epidemiologic and genomic data, we identified three to four distinct “cholera transmission units” within which cross-border cholera transmission has been more frequent. These units can be grouped into two major transmission clusters, one in Western Africa and bordering countries and one spanning the Central, Eastern, and Southern regions. Simulation studies show that these clusters can be used to assess the risk of international spread of introduced cholera strains and identify heterogeneities in the speed of international spread based on outbreak location. Our methods further allow us to infer cholera incidence attributable to specific lineages in the absence of sequencing data. This work has clear implications for cholera control.

title: Comprehensive classification of HCN1 variants linked to neurodevelopmental disorders with and without epilepsy
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
Hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated 1 (HCN1) channels mediate the cationic
                    I
                    h
                    current, a fundamental regulator of neuronal excitability and synaptic integration, and are predominantly expressed in the cortex and hippocampus. Although
                    HCN1
                    variants have been increasingly identified in patients with epilepsy, from milder forms to developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEE), genotype–phenotype correlations remain poorly defined. Here, we used patch-clamp electrophysiology and confocal imaging in HEK293 cells to functionally characterize 43
                    HCN1
                    variants identified in patients with neurodevelopmental disorders, with or without epilepsy. Based on biophysical properties, we established a classification system comprising four distinct functional classes: I) low or no current; II) hyperpolarizing shift in voltage dependence; III) depolarizing shift in voltage dependence; and IV) generation of an instantaneous current. The molecular basis for this classification was further interpreted using available cryo-EM structures of HCN1. Integration with clinical data from 50 patients revealed a striking correlation between functional class and clinical presentation. Loss-of-function variants prevailed among individuals with milder phenotypes or without epilepsy, with the latter distinctively clustering within the channel selectivity filter. In contrast, gain-of-function and mixed variants were predominantly associated with DEE. Finally, we demonstrate that allosteric modulators, including peptides NB6 and TRIP8b
                    nano
                    and the small molecule J&J12e, effectively normalize channel function across three of the four classes in vitro. These findings establish a biophysical framework for interpreting
                    HCN1
                    variants, demonstrating that the direction of channel dysfunction is a major determinant of epilepsy risk and severity, and providing a conceptual foundation for future class-based precision medicine approaches.

title: Patterns of implicit and explicit attitudes V: Increases in bias from 2021 to 2025
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
Between 2007 and 2020, implicit and explicit intergroup attitudes declined in bias steadily and were forecasted to continue toward attitude neutrality. But, since 2020, 5 y of new data (2021–2025) from 2.8 million U.S. respondents reveal that past trends have stalled or, in some cases, even reversed. The largest reversals in bias emerged for sexuality, transgender, race, and skin-tone bias which increased by 12 to 22% on implicit measures and by 24% to more than tripling on explicit measures. Age, disability, and body weight bias also increased, but at relatively slower rates. Breakpoint analyses showed that implicit attitudes were early indicators of change, reversing trend ~1 y earlier than explicit reports. For most topics, reversals were widespread across demographic groups and even extended to an international sample of 274,884 non-U.S. respondents. However, younger respondents (<20-y-old)—who had previously shown the largest
                    decreases
                    in bias—now showed the largest increases in bias; these trends also interacted with politics and gender (e.g., young conservative men were the most likely to increase). Exploratory analyses ruled out various single-cause explanations. Instead, we suggest that the best explanation is that 2020–2021 marked a turning point in the sociopolitical climate, whereby co-occurring existential threats from the COVID-19 pandemic, amplified economic insecurity, political sectarianism, and online toxicity prompted increases in intergroup bias. These data underscore how large populations of individual-level attitudes are continually shaped and altered by macro, societal-level events.

title: The purinergic receptor P2Y13 controls the activation and mode of division of adult ventricular–subventricular zone neural stem cells
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
The ventricular–subventricular zone (V-SVZ) is the most active germinal area in the mammalian brain and it continues to generate newborn neurons throughout life. This area harbors a population of neural stem cells (NSCs) that exist in different states of activation: quiescent NSCs, primed NSCs, and activated NSCs. There are currently few specific markers to effectively discern each state. Likewise, the molecular signals that control the transition from quiescence to activation remain largely unexplored, and the factors that controls whether dividing NSCs differentiate or self-renew are poorly understood. Here, we present evidence that the metabotropic P2Y
                    13
                    purinergic receptor plays a critical role in regulating adult neurogenesis. We found that P2Y
                    13
                    is specifically expressed in NSCs within the adult V-SVZ and that its levels can be used to distinguish quiescent from activated NSCs. P2Y
                    13
                    signaling promotes NSC activation, enhancing lineage progression as opposed to their self-renewal. Conversely, pharmacological blockade or genetic silencing of P2Y
                    13
                    receptors favors NSC quiescence. Thus, we consider the metabotropic P2Y
                    13
                    purinergic receptor a pivotal modulator of NSC dynamics.

title: Municipal sludge disposal emerges as a major, hidden, and rapidly growing atmospheric mercury source
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
Wastewater treatment greatly reduces mercury pollution in aquatic ecosystems but does not eliminate it. Here, we identify municipal sludge disposal as a major, long-overlooked atmospheric mercury source. In China, sludge disposal emitted
                    
                      
                        
                          42
                          
                            -
                            10
                          
                          
                            +
                            18
                          
                        
                      
                    
                    Mg in 2024, exceeding 10% of national anthropogenic emissions and ranking third after cement production and nonferrous metal smelting. These emissions have increased by nearly a thousandfold since the 1970s and are concentrated in densely populated urban areas, driven by the rapid expansion of sludge incineration, codisposal, and composting. Our findings reveal a cross-media pollution transfer embedded in sustainability transitions and call for sludge disposal to be incorporated into UNEP mercury budget and Minamata Convention assessments.

title: Entropic tightening of knots in granular chains under vibration
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Knots are common in long chains, from DNA and proteins to everyday strings, yet direct observation of knot dynamics is difficult. Using granular chains on vibrating platforms, we directly visualize knot dynamics and find that knot cores spontaneously tighten, a behavior observed across different knot types. We quantitatively explain spontaneous knot tightening using knot-tube theory: segments confined within the knot core experience entropic loss and tend to escape the core to gain conformational entropy. Although driven granular chains are not in thermodynamic equilibrium, their steady-state knot-size statistics are approximately captured by equilibrium statistical mechanics and Monte Carlo simulations. Analyses of state-transition probabilities and time-reversal asymmetry suggest a weak violation of detailed balance when the granular dynamics are projected onto the knot-size coordinate. Finally, we discuss the possible relevance of knot tightening to topoisomerase-mediated DNA unknotting.

title: A tetravalent bispecific protein enables targeted degradation of VCAM-1 and VEGFR for treatment of choroidal neovascularization
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Wet age-related macular degeneration (AMD), a leading cause of irreversible vision loss, is driven by pathological choroidal neovascularization (CNV). Although anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) therapies remain the clinical standard, their utility is constrained by incomplete responses in nearly 50% of patients and off-target risks—such as geographic atrophy—stemming from non-specific VEGF blockade. Here, we identify a robust correlation between vascular cell adhesion molecule-1 (VCAM-1) and VEGF/VEGF receptor (VEGFR) expression in aqueous humor from AMD patients and in murine CNV models. Thus, we engineered a tetravalent bispecific protein, RHV, by functionalizing an L-rhamnulose-1-phosphate aldolase scaffold with peptides that selectively bind VCAM-1 and the VEGFR on neovessels. The tetravalent design confers high apparent affinity, enhancing pathological endothelial targeting while sparing healthy retinal vasculature. RHV induces concurrent internalization and lysosomal degradation of both VCAM-1 and VEGFR via a head-to-tail binding mode, leading to sustained inhibition of the VEGF/VEGFR, PI3K/AKT and Apelin/APJ signaling pathways. In murine CNV models, a single intravitreal injection of RHV exhibits superior ocular retention and lesion penetration, achieving therapeutic efficacy comparable to aflibercept [a ligand-trap fusion protein for VEGF-A, VEGF-B and placental growth factor (PIGF)] at one-quarter of the molar dose. This dual-receptor degradation-based strategy represents a targeted and durable approach for treating ocular neovascularization.

title: Lead impairs long-term memory by disrupting mitochondrial redox homeostasis in Drosophila
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
Lead (Pb) exposure remains a major environmental risk factor for cognitive dysfunction, yet the cellular mechanisms underlying Pb-induced memory impairment are poorly understood. Here, we show that both developmental and adult-onset Pb exposure selectively disrupts protein-synthesis-dependent long-term memory (LTM) in
                    Drosophila melanogaster
                    while sparing other memory forms. Using a mitochondria-targeted redox biosensor (mito-roGFP2-Orp1), we found that Pb elevates mitochondrial oxidative stress and disrupts redox homeostasis in cholinergic neurons and in dorsal-anterior-lateral (DAL) neurons, a critical locus for LTM consolidation. Pb-induced redox imbalance suppresses training-induced de novo protein synthesis in DAL neurons, thereby impairing memory consolidation. Antioxidant treatment with epigallocatechin gallate restores mitochondrial redox balance and rescues LTM by reinstating activity-dependent protein synthesis in DAL neurons. These findings identify mitochondrial redox dysregulation as a key mechanism linking environmental Pb exposure to impaired memory consolidation. Our results further establish a genetically tractable platform for dissecting neurotoxic mechanisms and for evaluating antioxidant-based strategies to mitigate Pb-induced cognitive dysfunction.

title: Intrinsically motivated humans and agents in open-world exploration
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
What drives exploration? Understanding the intrinsic motivation to explore is a long-standing challenge in both cognitive science and AI. In this study, we directly compare adults, children aged 8 to 12 y, and AI agents exploring a complex, open-ended environment called Crafter (
                    1
                    ). We study how three common information-theoretic intrinsic objectives—entropy, information gain, and empowerment—relate to their behavior. We find that all three are positively correlated with human exploration progress for both children and adults, although entropy and empowerment are more strongly related to exploration progress in children than information gain. Furthermore, across agents and humans we observe that entropy initially increases rapidly, then plateaus, while empowerment increases continuously, suggesting that in early exploration they look for novel states, while in advanced exploration they look for states they can control. Finally, we find preliminary evidence that private speech about goals may aid exploration in children. Our data are available at
                    https://github.com/alyd/humans_in_crafter_data
                    .

title: A DPY19L2/FAM209-associated protein–Arp complex–CAPZA3 scaffold is essential for perinuclear theca assembly and fertilization
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
Fertilization is a fundamental biological process that enables the fusion of a spermatozoon with an oocyte to initiate embryonic development. However, the underlying mechanisms leading to fertilization failure remain poorly understood. Here, we demonstrated that the actin-related protein (Arp) family members ACTRT2 and ACTRT3 are essential for fertilization in both humans and mice, whereas ACTL10 is dispensable for fertility and the human-specific ACTL8 may play a role in early spermatogenesis. Ultrastructural and immunofluorescence analyses revealed that, during spermatogenesis, ACTRT2 or ACTRT3 deficiency disrupts the assembly of subacrosomal layer of the perinuclear theca (SAL-PT), leading to acrosome detachment and subsequent manchette abnormalities, which in turn impairs the formation of the postacrosomal sheath of the PT. These structural defects were accompanied by reduced abundance of the candidate sperm-borne oocyte-activating factors PAWP and PLCζ. Moreover, knockout of
                    Actrt2
                    or
                    Actrt3
                    severely impaired spermatozoa’s ability to penetrate the zona pellucida during in vitro fertilization. Mechanistically, ACTRT2, ACTRT3, ACTL7A, ACTL7B, and ACTL9 form a testis-enriched Arp complex in the SAL-PT and maintain the stability of one another. This complex interacts with the PT protein CAPZA3, which subsequently binds and stabilizes PLCζ. Additionally, the Arp complex interacts with DPY19L2/FAM209-associated proteins to mediate acrosome anchoring to the nuclear envelope. Therefore, these findings established a sequential DPY19L2/FAM209-associated protein–Arp complex–CAPZA3 scaffold extending from the nuclear envelope to the acrosome that is indispensable for fertilization. Collectively, we defined a previously unidentified structural and molecular framework for fertilization and provided insights into the diagnosis and treatment of fertilization failure.

title: Dynamic virulence decomposition disentangles host and pathogen contributions over the course of infection
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
Decomposing virulence into host and pathogen effects is key to understanding how virulence is generated during infection, and how host and pathogen contributions evolve over time. Conventional virulence decomposition is, however, not designed to quantify how these contributions vary throughout an infection. Building on conventional virulence decomposition, we developed a dynamic framework that integrates disease space analysis to quantify these changing contributions. We applied this framework to existing data from house finches (
                    Haemorhous mexicanus
                    ) experimentally infected with the emerging bacterial pathogen,
                    Mycoplasma gallisepticum
                    , examining two biologically meaningful infection phases: an early phase dominated by innate immune responses and a later phase in which the adaptive immune response is fully activated. Our analyses revealed that virulence components evolved differently across infection phases, with pathogen exploitation, per-parasite-pathogenicity (PPP), and host resistance each exhibiting distinct trajectories. These findings corroborated several known evolutionary patterns, while also revealing the evolution of increased PPP in this system. In contrast, the apparent evolution of host tolerance inferred from aggregated peak measurements was not supported by phase-specific analyses, demonstrating that aggregated and phase-specific measures can provide different mechanistic insights into virulence. By linking conventional virulence decomposition with disease space analysis, our dynamic virulence decomposition framework provides a general approach for quantifying how host and pathogen processes shape virulence over the course of infection.

title: Maize genetic diversity is largely unstructured by human ethnolinguistic diversity in its center of origin
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
Population structure and environmental features often capture major axes of genetic variation in many species. Yet the impacts of human activity often remain unquantified. For domesticated species that rely on human activity for survival and dispersal, human movements and cultural differences may play key roles patterning genetic diversity. Maize is a staple crop of enormous cultural importance to indigenous peoples of the Americas, but cannot survive or disperse without farmers. Using publicly available genotyping and passport data from approximately 2,000 traditional maize varieties, more than 500 whole genome sequences of humans from Mexico, and indigenous linguistic maps, we quantify anthropogenic effects on maize genetic diversity in the Americas. Maize shows very little overall structure, highlighting the effectiveness of indigenous farmers in moving and mixing maize populations. While principal components of maize diversity show meaningful correlations to human genetic diversity, our linear modeling suggests little additional impact of human population structure beyond shared geography. Though differences in maize diversity are often patterned by language locally, we find only weak genome-wide effects at larger spatial scales. Despite the relatively weak global signal of anthropogenic effects, linguistic Genome-wide association, outlier
                    
                      
                        
                          F
                          
                            ST
                          
                        
                      
                    
                    analyses, and selection scans identified loci associated with specific languages. Leveraging landscape-level sequencing data, we highlight how anthropogenic factors have shaped patterns of maize genetic diversity across Mesoamerica.

title: An aggregation-prone region in talin controls talin self-interactions and regulates integrin adhesion complex dynamics
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Talin is a mechanosensitive scaffold that couples integrins to the actin cytoskeleton and coordinates signaling at integrin adhesion complexes. A second integrin-binding site (IBS2) has been proposed within the R11–R12 region of the talin rod, although the molecular basis of this interaction has remained unclear. Here, we show that talin R11 contains a cryptic aggregation-prone region (APR) embedded within Helix50. Mechanical unfolding of R11 exposes this motif, enabling high-affinity talin–talin interactions and force-dependent self-association. The isolated APR forms amyloid-like fibers in vitro, and APR-disrupting gatekeeper mutations suppress fiber formation, talin self-association, and cellular recruitment. We therefore designate this motif Aggregation-Prone Region 1 (APR1). Mitochondrial-targeting experiments demonstrate that APR1-dependent recruitment occurs in cells independently of focal adhesions and integrins. APR1 overlaps the vinculin-binding site in Helix50, and vinculin disrupts preexisting talin assemblies, revealing a mechano-chaperone function for vinculin. Disruption of APR1-mediated self-association does not impair adhesion formation but instead generates larger, more talin-rich adhesions with altered assembly dynamics and signaling properties, indicating a role for APR1 in regulating adhesion remodeling. Together, these findings identify force-dependent talin self-association as a mechanism in mechanotransduction and suggest that the region previously designated IBS2 functions primarily as an aggregation-prone regulatory element.

title: USP46 restrains K63-linked polyubiquitination–dependent aggregation and activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in lupus nephritis
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: The activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome necessitates its aggregation within the dispersed trans-Golgi network (dTGN) and subsequent transport from the dTGN to the microtubule organizing center (MTOC), a process facilitated by HDAC6. However, the regulatory mechanisms governing the formation of NLRP3 aggregates remain insufficiently understood. In this study, we demonstrate that proteasome impairment induces polyubiquitination and aggregation of NLRP3 at the MTOC. We demonstrate ubiquitin-specific protease 46 (USP46) as a key factor that recognizes NLRP3 as a substrate and restricts nondegradative K63-linked polyubiquitination at lysine residue K930, thereby preventing excessive aggregation, transport to the MTOC, and inflammasome activation. Furthermore, myeloid-specific knockout of USP46 exacerbates renal injury and inflammation in both lipopolysaccharide-induced-induced endotoxic shock and pristane-induced lupus nephritis models. Our findings provide insights into the regulatory mechanisms underlying the aggresomal activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome.

title: Multifunctional multiphysics metamaterials via decomposition-based multiobjective optimization design
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Metamaterials offer unprecedented control over physical fields through their microstructure, but current design methods cannot meet the demands of scenarios involving active sources, multiphysics field coupling, and multifunctional requirements. Moreover, existing approaches are generally developed for specific functions, making it difficult to integrate different functionalities and select the functional priorities within a single structure. To overcome these limitations, this study presents a systematic inverse design framework for multifunctional multiphysics metamaterials via multiobjective optimization. To uniformly explore the Pareto front, which clearly exhibits trade-offs among functionalities and facilitates the selection of functional priorities, we employ dynamic normalization into the decomposition-based multiobjective evolutionary algorithm. A robust anisotropic unit-cell database is constructed and used for generating metamaterials with optimized microstructures for multifunctionality. Three complex cases are studied that can simultaneously achieve mechanical cloaking plus stress minimization, thermal cloaking plus stress minimization, and direct current cloaking plus thermal stress minimization. Furthermore, the proposed framework is employed in potential engineering problems, for example, to realize mechanical cloaking by embedding functional components in structural materials, while minimizing the surrounding stress on functional components for mechanical protection when the assembled structures are compressed, thereby decoupling the interaction between functional and structural components. This systematic framework expands the capabilities of metamaterials in complex multiphysics coupling, offering a robust blueprint for future intelligent, structurally and functionally integrated systems.

title: Effector-triggered stomatal immunity prevents leaf invasion by bacterial pathogens
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
The phytopathogen
                    Pseudomonas syringae
                    must enter the leaf interior through natural openings such as stomata to cause disease. Plants restrict pathogen entry into the leaf through non–self-recognition–driven stomatal closure.
                    P. syringae
                    counters this stomatal immunity by deploying a range of toxins and effectors. Here, we show that stomatal immunity in
                    Arabidopsis thaliana
                    is reinforced upon recognition of the ubiquitous
                    P. syringae
                    type III effector AvrE1 by the resistance protein CAR1.
                    CAR1
                    expression is enriched in guard cells, and its activation prolongs the effective duration of stomatal immunity. We also show that CAR1 prevents the invasion of leaf tissue by natural isolates of
                    P. syringae
                    , demonstrating that stomatal immunity provides a broadly significant barrier to host accessibility by
                    P. syringae
                    that carry the conserved effector AvrE1.

title: Rapid, voxel-based 3D printing with yield-stress fluid inks
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Despite decades of progress, 3D printing still presents trade-offs in what materials can be printed and at what resolutions, speeds, and part volumes. We introduce direct ink additive lithography, or DIAL, to alleviate these trade-offs when printing with yield-stress, complex fluid inks used to print functional materials. DIAL combines translational photopatterning with ink sheet deposition for rapid, voxel-based 3D printing. Using model DIAL inks with kilopascal-scale yield stresses, we evaluate how ink rheology influences printing and compare DIAL against digital light processing (DLP) and direct ink writing (DIW). Since DIAL enables fast, high-throughput, support-free, and large-area printing, we showcase its broad potential for producing functional materials by printing multiscale architected, multimaterial, structural electrolyte, and hydrogel structures that are difficult if not impossible to 3D print today.

title: A biofilm-derived peptide as an underwater adhesive
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
Wet adhesives that perform under water have broad applications in industrial and biomedical settings. To date, molecular designs for underwater adhesives have largely been inspired by marine animals including mussels and barnacles. Here, we propose bacterial biofilms as an alternative source of inspiration for underwater adhesives. Specifically, we demonstrate the application potential of a peptide derived from biofilms formed by the notorious pathogen
                    Vibrio cholerae
                    . We characterize the ability of this biofilm-derived peptide to adsorb onto various surfaces and to glue wet surfaces by using a combination of confocal microscopy, molecular dynamics simulations, atomic force microscopy, lap shear tests, and spectroscopic tools. We further show that the peptide can coaggregate with microspheres acting as an effective flocculant. Our results open new design possibilities for underwater adhesives inspired by natural biofilms.

title: Oxygen-mediated projection microstereolithography for sub–100-μm zirconia dental veneers
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: High-resolution vat photopolymerization of ceramics is constrained by light scattering, which broadens cured features, and by shallow penetration, which limits interlayer bonding. This trade-off is particularly damaging for microscale structures such as no-preparation dental veneers. We introduce an oxygen-mediated projection microstereolithography strategy in which an oxygen-permeable release film creates an interfacial inhibition field in high-solid–loading zirconia slurry. Rather than uniformly reducing curing, oxygen preferentially filters low-dose scattered light at pattern edges while preserving curing in the projected core. This anisotropic inhibition reshapes the accuracy-depth trade-off, enabling optimized multilayer printing of thin-wall zirconia. The process enabled reproducible fabrication of ∼80-micrometer zirconia veneers with high trueness, improved marginal adaptation, and handling-related strength comparable to substantially thicker milled veneers. The approach provides the potential for minimally invasive dental restoration and a general strategy for high-resolution additive manufacturing of strongly scattering ceramic suspensions.

title: On-going retinal neuronal degeneration despite clinical stability in glaucoma
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Glaucoma, a leading cause of irreversible blindness, involves progressive retinal ganglion cell loss. Early detection of this neurodegeneration is critical, yet current clinical methods often identify disease only after substantial damage has occurred. This preliminary study used high-resolution adaptive optics–optical coherence tomography (AO-OCT) to track individual retinal ganglion cells in patients and healthy volunteers over 3 to 5 years. Results revealed higher neurodegeneration in glaucoma compared to normal aging. We observed 4.16 to 6.86% annual decrease in cell density in glaucoma, far exceeding the 0.27% cell loss rate observed in the healthy volunteer group. Critically, AO-OCT detected progression significantly earlier, identifying cell loss 0.74 years before conventional OCT and 1.49 years before visual field testing. These findings demonstrate AO-OCT as a more sensitive tool capable of monitoring glaucomatous damage with superior precision, potentially representing a major advancement over current clinical imaging.

title: Persistent bistability of Nordic Seas overflow waters over 800,000 years
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: The stability of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is a major uncertainty in projections of future climate. However, direct evidence for AMOC tipping behavior on orbital timescales remains scarce. Here, we reconstruct the strength of Iceland-Scotland Overflow Water, a key lower branch of the deep Atlantic circulation, over the past 800,000 years by combining 12 current-speed records from North Atlantic sediment cores with a data-driven hybrid model. The resulting reconstruction reveals persistent alternation between weak (glacial) and strong (interglacial) circulation modes, pervasive millennial-scale variability within both regimes, and systematic asymmetry between weak-to-strong recoveries and strong-to-weak collapses. Threshold and phase-space analyses show that regime shifts occur within a narrow window of atmospheric carbon dioxide and sea level and often follow hysteresis-like loops. Although bistability persists throughout the last 800,000 years, its sensitivity and timing evolve through time. These findings provide long-term, high-resolution, data-driven constraints on the bistability of Nordic Seas overflow waters and its implications for AMOC resilience in a warming world.

title: Clinically derived micro- and nanoplastic uptake drives spatiotemporally confined metabolic stress revealed by bond-selective imaging
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Although microplastics and nanoplastics (MPs/NPs) are pervasive environmental contaminants, our understanding of cellular toxicity remains incomplete, as adverse effects are often attributed to long-term intracellular accumulation, while the spatiotemporal onset of cellular damage remains poorly defined. Here, we use chemical bond–selective stimulated Raman scattering (SRS) microscopy and cell models that decouple continuous exposure from intracellular retention to directly visualize clinically derived MP/NP-cell interactions. Cellular stress occurs primarily during MP/NP exposure, accompanied by alterations in lipid droplet (LD) composition. In contrast, following extracellular removal, intracellularly retained MP/NP become largely inert, with recovery of lipid metabolism and cellular functions. Lipidomics identifies arachidonic acid (AA) as a key dysregulated metabolite, and SRS imaging further reveals transient, spatially confined AA enrichment in MP/NP–proximal LDs during uptake. Phospholipid coating of MP/NP attenuates LD alterations and cytotoxicity while preserving particle internalization, establishing uptake-driven metabolic stress, rather than long-term intracellular retention, as a primary source of MP/NP–induced damage.

title: Local translational program at the muscle-tendon junction endows domain identity in muscle syncytia
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: How cells establish specialized subdomains is a fundamental question in cell and tissue biology. Skeletal muscle fibers, among the largest cells in the body, are multinucleated and form distinct regions such as the neuromuscular and myotendinous junctions (MTJs), the latter forming a critical interface between muscle and tendon that transmits contractile force. While transcriptional heterogeneity among myonuclei has been described, whether local translation contributes to domain identity remains unknown, largely due to the lack of tools for domain-specific manipulation. Here, we introduce MTJ-AAV, a viral system that enables selective genetic targeting of MTJ myonuclei. This approach allowed MTJ-specific ribosome tagging and revealed extensive translational regulation underlying MTJ biology and its remodeling during exercise. Untranslated regions of these transcripts were sufficient to control regionalized translation. Notably, the Krüpper-like factor–family transcription factors emerged as translationally up-regulated targets at the MTJ, where they drive local gene expression. Our findings establish local translation as a key layer of subcellular specialization and provide a versatile toolkit for dissecting spatial molecular regulation within muscle syncytia.

title: A functional connectome identifies vulnerability to cognitive decline and Alzheimer’s disease progression
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
Identifying the neurobiological basis of cognitive vulnerability is essential for preventing Alzheimer’s disease (AD). We derived the Alzheimer’s Resilience-Vulnerability Connectome (ARC) by contrasting SuperAgers (SA), an extreme phenotype of preserved late-life memory, with AD using resting-state fMRI. ARC distinguished SA from AD in a discovery cohort (
                    N
                     = 290; AUC = 0.85) and replicated independently (
                    N
                     = 143), involving prefrontal, temporal, and insular networks and associating with brain age. Applied to cognitively unimpaired adults (discovery:
                    N
                     = 818; replication:
                    N
                     = 497), ARC-based subtyping revealed SA-like and AD-like subgroups with comparable baseline cognition but divergent longitudinal trajectories. AD-like individuals exhibited faster cognitive decline, greater amyloid-β accumulation, and higher AD conversion risk. Exploratory GWAS nominated
                    CLYBL
                    and
                    FRMD6
                    as candidate novel loci associated with the subtype difference. These findings suggest that ARC captures a continuous connectomic dimension of cognitive aging spanning SA, cognitively typical aging, and AD, highlighting the potential of functional connectomic variation for early risk stratification in AD.

title: Stony coral symbioses show variable responses to future ocean conditions
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Coral reefs support over a quarter of marine species and nearly a billion people worldwide but are also among the ecosystems most threatened by anthropogenic impacts. There is long-standing debate about whether coral symbioses will be disrupted or respond adaptively under future ocean conditions. Using a factorial 2.5-year future-ocean mesocosm experiment across eight coral species representing the major coral lineages, we tracked symbiont community shifts within replicate fragments from the same individual coral. Some corals exhibited stochastic divergence, whereas others showed deterministic shifts in symbiont community composition. Heat stress generally reduced symbiont diversity and promoted predictable restructuring, consistent with deterministic adaptation to moderate thermal stress but stochastic accumulation of diversity under extreme conditions. We propose that adaptive and stochastic responses represent endpoints along a continuum of host-orchestrated symbiont sorting. This study bridges coral reef ecology with broader host-microbiome theory, offering an integrated perspective on how symbiotic systems may respond to environmental change.

title: METTL3-mediated m6A modification of DNMT1 enhances ovarian cancer progression
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
High-grade serous ovarian carcinoma (HGSOC), the most lethal subtype of ovarian cancer, is often diagnosed at advanced stages and remains associated with poor clinical outcome. In this study, we identify a critical oncogenic role of the RNA methyltransferase METTL3 and the
                    N
                    6
                    -methyladenosine (m
                    6
                    A) RNA modification pathway in HGSOC. Suppression of METTL3, either genetically or pharmacologically, and depletion of its binding partner METTL14 impair ovarian cancer proliferation and tumor progression. Mechanistically, we show that METTL3-mediated m
                    6
                    A deposition enhances the translation of DNA methyltransferase 1 (DNMT1), the primary maintenance DNA methyltransferase responsible for preserving genome-wide methylation patterns and silencing tumor suppressor genes. Pharmacological inhibition of DNMT1 induces widespread DNA hypomethylation and up-regulation of the tumor suppressors TNFAIP3 and FBXO32. Consistently, METTL3 suppression reduces DNMT1 abundance and derepresses TNFAIP3 and FBXO32 expression. Knockdown and rescue studies further reveal that DNMT1 primarily mediates METTL3-dependent regulation of cell migration, whereas the antiproliferative effects of METTL3 suppression are likely driven by additional downstream targets. Collectively, these findings identify the m
                    6
                    A-METTL3-DNMT1 axis as a mechanistic link between RNA and DNA methylation pathways and a potential therapeutic vulnerability in HGSOC.

title: Enigmatic HCl detections as a potential signature of igneous activity on Mars
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Mars is reputed to lack ongoing volcanic activity. However, marsquakes were revealed recently, and clues to volcanism younger than tens of million years have accumulated. While sulfur dioxide, so far undetected, could testify to ongoing eruptive activity, evidence of active magma chambers may be better identified by seepage of halogen gases, such as hydrogen chloride (HCl). Observations by Atmospheric Chemistry Suite led to the widespread observations of HCl at part-per-billion levels in the atmosphere of Mars during the warm perihelion period, attributed to aerosol-atmospheric sources. Here, we report HCl detections during the cold aphelion season that are isolated in the Alba Mons region. We also identify fresh and narrow (<1 meter) fissures in this area, which we interpret to be potential HCl pathways rooted into magmatic bodies at depth. Our results are best explained by ongoing igneous processes in the Martian interior.

title: Cooper’s Ferry/Nipéhe, stratigraphic integrity, and confirming early inland dispersal: Evaluating peopling of the Americas modeling
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Statistical models shape debates over the timing and geography of the initial peopling of the Americas, but their value depends on testing their assumptions against archaeological evidence. We examine the Apparent Stratigraphic Integrity Index (ASI), used to infer postdepositional mixing at Late Pleistocene sites and support a relatively late occupation of temperate North America. ASI describes vertical discontinuity in binned artifact-frequency profiles; it does not directly measure artifact movement or stratigraphic integrity. At Cooper’s Ferry/Nipéhe, Idaho, the 5-centimeter absolute-elevation bins used to calculate ASI do not reflect the actual stratigraphic positions of artifacts across the irregular LU2 surface on which LU3 loess accumulated. The resulting ASI value cannot support claims of large-scale vertical mixing. Independent chronological, stratigraphic, pedogenic, archaeological, and excavation evidence supports the integrity of the ∼16,000–calibrated-years-before-the-present occupation. Cooper’s Ferry/Nipéhe provides early inland evidence expected under coastal-migration models, showing that models should be evaluated against archaeological evidence rather than used to override it.

title: Progressive shifts in soil respiration response to long-term nitrogen enrichment across global forests and grasslands
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
Soil stores the largest pool of actively cycling carbon (C) on land, and its dynamics under global changes are critical for projecting climate feedbacks. Global nitrogen (N) deposition has more than doubled since the 1860s; however, the temporal dynamics of soil C emissions under prolonged N deposition are poorly understood. Here, using a global time-series dataset compiled from 38 long-term experiments in forests and grasslands, we find that the response of soil respiration (Rs) to N addition systematically shifts from a transient increase persisting for approximately 2 y to a sustained suppression over time (mean effect = −6%; 95% CI = [−10%, −3%]). Rs in forests and grasslands followed consistent nonlinear trajectories, characterized by a rapid initial decline in the magnitude of the response, which progressively leveled off. Notably, suppression of Rs emerged when cumulative N inputs exceeded a threshold of ~100 kg N ha
                    −1
                    . Consequently, the suppression was both stronger and occurred more rapidly under high-level N additions (>50 kg N ha
                    −1
                    y
                    −1
                    ). These temporal dynamics were associated with N-induced soil acidification and related changes in microbial properties. Overall, these findings indicate that accurate prediction of land–atmosphere C fluxes under global change requires models to capture the reported temporal dynamics.

title: Codfishes survived essential gene loss by functionally co-opting freshwater ovulatory pathways to marine egg hydration
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
Adaptive evolution associated with dispensable gene loss is widespread in the animal kingdom. However, loss of genes essential for embryonic survival and the mechanisms that evolved to bypass negative selection and extinction are less well known. Here, we show that all Gadiformes, an ecologically dominant order of codfishes, lost the
                    aqp1ab
                    -type genes that are essential for the formation of hydrated pelagic eggs and embryonic survival of marine teleosts in oceanic environments. Despite such gene loss, codfishes produce some of the most highly hydrated pelagic eggs of all marine teleosts. To resolve this apparent paradox, we initially confirmed that the mechanisms of osmotic drive are conserved with other pelagic-egg-producing marine teleosts, and then conducted comparative transcript analyses of aquaporin water channels in distantly-related freshwater and marine teleosts. This uncovered Aqp4-type channels that have been chromosomally linked to the Aqp1-type channels in jawed vertebrate genomes for >450 million years as the primary candidates. Using immunolocalization, functional assays, and inhibition experiments with zebrafish and Atlantic cod as model organisms, we show that short isoforms of Aqp4 are required for egg ovulation in more ancestral lineages of freshwater teleosts and were recruited to the oocyte hydration pathway of codfishes. By contrast, the oldest and most modern lineages of marine teleosts producing pelagic eggs still utilize the
                    aqp1ab
                    genes for egg hydration. Our data thus reveal that codfishes survived essential gene loss by functionally co-opting freshwater ovulatory pathways to marine egg hydration.

title: Modified Newtonian Dynamics and galaxy clusters
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: First proposed by Milgrom in 1983 as an alternative to the standard Cold Dark Matter (CDM) paradigm, Modified Newtonian Dynamics (MOND) has gained renewed momentum in light of persistent nondetections of exotic dark matter particles and growing tensions facing CDM on galactic scales. While MOND perfectly reproduces galactic rotation curves, it encounters notable challenges in explaining the equilibrium of galaxy clusters. Although it reduces the overall dark matter budget in these massive systems, an unidentified mass component remains required. This paper investigates the hypothesis that this missing mass is baryonic: composed of nonradiating ordinary matter such as stellar remnants, gas too diffuse to initiate star formation, or compact, ultra-dense clouds of cold molecular gas with low volume filling factors. Using a sample of 106 clusters mapped in X-rays, emitted by the hot intracluster medium composing most of the visible mass, we derive first the total mass within the Newtonian dynamics, assuming hydrostatic equilibrium and spherical symmetry. Then, with the modified Poisson equation, we reconstruct the spatial distribution of the invisible missing matter within the MOND framework. In the sample, the relaxed systems harboring cooling flows, known as cool-core clusters, have the highest peaks of dark missing mass. Its density profile reveals a pronounced central concentration bounded by a steep truncation immediately beyond a core radius of 20 to 30 kpc, confirming previous studies. MOND reduces the necessary dynamical mass by a factor of 4 to 10. The residual missing mass is proportional to the total gas mass, being roughly twice lower.

title: Profile of Françoise Combes
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Françoise Combes’s childhood curiosity motivated her to pursue a career in science. Her studies in physics at the École Normale Supérieure in Paris eventually led her to focus on astrophysics. With help from mentors, such as astrophysicists Evry Schatzman and Pierre Encrenaz, Combes has had a distinguished career in astrophysics. She is renowned for her work studying the formation and evolution of galaxies and their dynamics and her research on dark matter. In her Inaugural Article, she describes her latest work exploring alternatives to dark matter.

title: A high robustness decoding technique for ultrasound modulated electroencephalogram
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Ultrasound-modulated electroencephalography (USMEEG) has become a vital tool in neuroscience because it integrates millimeter-level spatial resolution with millisecond-level temporal resolution. However, under extremely complex scenarios, excessively strong or weak acoustoelectric signal coupling leads to severe distortion in USMEEG decoded signals. To address this, we developed a highly robust decoding algorithm based on the ultrasound pulse repetition frequency and introduced the acoustoelectric modulation ratio (AMR) to quantify different modulation scenarios. Across numerical simulations, phantoms, and validation using human steady-state visual evoked potential signals with data-level acoustoelectric coupling across 10 volunteers, the focused ultrasound phased array achieved an encoding spatial resolution of 0.79 millimeters. The proposed algorithm significantly outperformed four traditional methods, exhibiting higher precision under weak modulation (0 < AMR ≤ 0.6), moderate modulation (0.6 < AMR ≤ 1), and over modulation (AMR > 1) conditions, with average decoding correlations reaching 0.84, 0.90, and 0.89. This highly robust technique expands USMEEG applications and provides a technical foundation for high-performance noninvasive brain-computer interfaces.
